name: Niacinamide

lead: Niacinamide (nicotinamide) is the amide form of vitamin B3 and a staple ingredient in cosmetic serums and moisturizers. Typical claims include improved barrier function, reduced oil appearance and pore prominence, calmer redness and a more even tone.
Clinical studies support modest benefits for hyperpigmentation, barrier function and some inflammatory acne, but effect sizes are generally small and vary between formulations.

paras: Niacinamide is a precursor of NAD+ and NADP+, coenzymes central to cellular energy and repair. In skin it increases ceramide and barrier lipid synthesis, reduces sebum output and interferes with the transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes, helping to lighten uneven pigment.

It is generally very well tolerated. Occasional flushing, itching or irritation occurs, especially at higher concentrations or in poorly formulated products. It is sold freely as a cosmetic ingredient.

lead: Niacinamide, also called nicotinamide, is the amide form of vitamin B3. It is found in foods such as yeast, meat, milk and green vegetables, is sold as a dietary supplement and medication, and is incorporated into cosmetic serums, moisturizers and cleansers.[1] Within cells it is a precursor of the coenzymes NAD+ and NADP+, which take part in many oxidation-reduction reactions.[1] Unlike nicotinic acid (niacin), it does not cause skin flushing at ordinary doses.[1]

In skin care it is promoted for improving barrier function, reducing sebum, evening skin tone and calming redness.[2][3] Reviews describe antipruritic, antimicrobial, vasoactive, photoprotective, sebostatic and lightening effects that depend on concentration and on how well the compound is delivered into skin.[3][4] A 2025 Delphi consensus of 62 dermatologists included niacinamide among the ingredients cosmetic dermatologists frequently recommend, for redness and dark spots.[5]

Published human trials are mostly small, often industry-linked, and use short treatment periods; one 2014 review noted that existing data were not sufficient for a scientifically founded evaluation of its therapeutic use even while describing the prospects as interesting.[3] Outside cosmetics, oral nicotinamide is used to treat pellagra and has been studied for non-melanoma skin cancer prevention and glaucoma.[1]
infobox: Nicotinamide, vitamin B3, nicotinic acid amide
Sold freely as a cosmetic ingredient and supplement; on the WHO Essential Medicines List

paras: Topical niacinamide is marketed for oil control and pore appearance, barrier support, redness, uneven tone and signs of ageing.[2][3] The 2025 dermatologist consensus assigned it to redness and dark spots.[5] A review on dermal delivery describes brightening, anti-ageing and barrier-protective roles.[2]

Oral nicotinamide is the preferred treatment for pellagra, the niacin deficiency disease, because it avoids niacin's flushing.[1] Wikipedia reports that nicotinamide cream is used for acne, that oral doses of 500 to 1000 mg daily reduced the risk of non-melanoma skin cancers in people at high risk, and that it is under investigation for glaucoma but is not approved for that use.[1] Reviews also cover topical use in dermatitis, acne vulgaris and actinic keratosis.[2]

Evidence is described as most developed for skin tone, barrier function and sebum. In a 2002 British Journal of Dermatology study, niacinamide reduced melanin transfer in laboratory models, and in clinical portions a 5 percent niacinamide moisturizer was compared with vehicle in 18 subjects with hyperpigmentation, and 2 percent niacinamide with sunscreen was tested in 120 subjects with facial tanning.[6] A 2005 randomized trial in 50 white female subjects assessed effects on wrinkles, yellowing and elasticity in ageing facial skin, building on earlier studies reporting improvements in hyperpigmented spots and red blotchiness.[7] A 2006 randomized trial examined 2 percent niacinamide and facial sebum production.[8]

Wikipedia summarises that 2 percent topical nicotinamide applied for two to four weeks lowered the sebum excretion rate, and that in vitro it raises ceramide synthesis in keratinocytes.[1] Reviews caution that results depend on formulation and skin penetration.[2] The dermatologist consensus noted that most consensus ingredients were supported by level 1b or 2b evidence while some rested on expert opinion.[5]

Randomized and controlled trials of topical niacinamide have examined skin pigmentation and tanning (the 2002 study of Japanese women, with 18- and 120-subject arms),[6] ageing facial skin in 50 female subjects (2005),[7] sebum production with 2 percent niacinamide (2006),[8] and acne, including a 2024 split-face randomized trial of a ceramide and niacinamide moisturizer added to anti-acne treatment.[9] A 2025 randomized double-blind trial compared niosomal and conventional tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams with hydroquinone in melasma,[10] and a 2021 randomized trial of scalp antioxidant application assessed shedding over 24 weeks.[11] A 2023 randomized study evaluated niacinamide body emollients in mild atopic dermatitis.[12]

Registered trials include a planned comparison of topical vitamin C and niacinamide for melasma (n=100, not yet recruiting) and studies of oral nicotinamide in glaucoma (n=58), kidney conditions, ataxia telangiectasia and cardiac surgery injury.[13][14][15] Reviews of the literature are available on mechanisms, clinical evidence and delivery strategies.[2][3][4][12]

Reviews describe topical niacinamide as well tolerated and safe.[3] Occasional flushing, itching or irritation has been reported with higher concentrations or particular formulations.[2] For oral use, Wikipedia reports minimal side effects, liver problems at high doses (acute liver toxicity documented in at least one case above 3,000 mg per day), a contraindication in liver disease, and safety at normal amounts in pregnancy.[1] A US antiperspirant label containing niacinamide advises consulting a doctor before use in people with kidney disease, although that warning concerns the product rather than the ingredient alone.[16]

In cells nicotinamide is converted via a salvage pathway into NAD+ and NADP+.[1] Pharmacological reviews describe inhibition of the enzyme PARP-1 and effects on NF-kappaB-mediated transcription of signalling molecules.[3] Laboratory work reports suppressed transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes,[6] increased ceramide synthesis,[1] and reduced Cutibacterium acnes-induced activation of toll-like receptor 2 with lower interleukin-8 production.[1]

Nicotinamide consists of a pyridine ring with a primary amide at the 3 position and is the amide of nicotinic acid. Industrially it is produced enzymatically from nicotinonitrile; Wikipedia gives a worldwide sales figure of 31,000 tons in 2014.[1]

Wikipedia states that nicotinamide was discovered between 1935 and 1937 and that it is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1] Its use in cosmetics grew through published trials from the early 2000s, including the 2002 pigmentation study, which has been cited several hundred times.[6]

On T Nation, niacinamide appears mostly as an oral supplement rather than a skin product. Posters list it in stacks for brain function and anxiety, in hormone-related troubleshooting threads, and in cholesterol discussions where one poster states that niacinamide, unlike niacin, does not affect cholesterol.[17][18][19][20][21]

lore.intro: In the forum material reviewed here, niacinamide is discussed less as a facial serum and more as an oral supplement in cognitive, mood and hormone-support stacks on T Nation.[17][20]
